'''James Mills Peirce''' (May 1, 1834<ref name="case" /> – March 21, 1906<ref name="cult">{{cite journal| first= Hubert| last= Kennedy| journal= [[Historia Mathematica]]| title= James Mills Peirce and the Cult of Quaternions| year= 1979| volume= 6| issue= 4| pages= 423–429| url= https://hubertkennedy.angelfire.com/Peirce.pdf | type=Six Articles on James Mills Peirce (2003) | doi=10.1016/0315-0860(79)90028-4| doi-access= free}}</ref>) was an [[Americans|American]] mathematician and educator.<ref name="case">{{cite journal| first= Hubert| last= Kennedy| author-link1= Hubert Kennedy |title= The Case for James Mills Peirce| journal= [[Journal of Homosexuality]] | volume= 4| number= 2| date= Winter 1978| pages= 179–184| type=Six Articles on James Mills Peirce (2003) | url= https://hubertkennedy.angelfire.com/Peirce.pdf| doi=10.1300/j082v04n02_04| pmid= 368227}}</ref> He taught at [[Harvard University]] for almost 50 years.<ref name="towards">{{cite journal| first= Hubert| last= Kennedy| journal= [[Historia Mathematica]]| title= Towards a Biography of James Mills Peirce| year= 1979| volume= 6| pages= 195–201| url= https://hubertkennedy.angelfire.com/Peirce.pdf | type=Six Articles on James Mills Peirce (2003) }}</ref>

==Early life and family==
Peirce was born May 1, 1834, in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Whittemore |first=J. K. |date=13 July 1906 |title=James Mills Peirce |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1633643 |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=24 |issue=602 |pages=40–48 |doi=10.1126/science.24.602.40 |jstor=1633643|pmid=17811032 |bibcode=1906Sci....24...40W }}</ref> He was the eldest son of Sarah Hunt (Mills)<ref name="towards" /> Peirce and [[Benjamin Peirce]] (1809–1880), a professor of astronomy and mathematics at [[Harvard University]].<ref name="case" /> The family was considered part of the [[Boston Brahmin]] elite class. The surname is pronounced to rhyme with "{{audio|en-us-purse.ogg|purse}}".<ref>{{cite web| url= http://www.iupui.edu/~peirce/news/1_3/13_4x.htm#pronunciation | title= Note on the Pronunciation of 'Peirce'| publisher= Peirce Project Newsletter| volume= 1| number= 3/4| date= December 1994| website= iupui.edu}}</ref> Benjamin Peirce's father, also named [[Benjamin Peirce (librarian)|Benjamin]], was librarian at Harvard.<ref name="reputations">{{cite news| first= Hubert| last= Kennedy| work= [[Harvard Magazine]]| title= Reputations reconsidered | date= November–December 1982| volume= 85| number= 2| pages= 62–64| url= https://hubertkennedy.angelfire.com/Peirce.pdf| type=Six Articles on James Mills Peirce (2003) }}</ref> James had four younger siblings; one brother was philosopher, logician and professor [[Charles Sanders Peirce]] (1839–1914).<ref name="towards" /> Another brother was [[Herbert H. D. Peirce|Herbert Henry Davis Peirce]] (1849–1916) who was the First Secretary of the American Embassy in [[Saint Petersburg]], [[Russia]], at the end of the 19th century.<ref name="cult" />

J. M. Peirce graduated from [[Harvard College]] in 1853.<ref name="case" /> While an undergraduate at Harvard, he was a member of the [[Hasty Pudding Club]].<ref name="case" /> He attended Harvard's law school for one year.<ref name="towards" /> In 1857, he enrolled at the university's [[Harvard Divinity School|Divinity School]] and graduated in 1859.<ref name="towards" />[[File:James Mills Peirce.jpg|thumb]]

==Career==
Like his father, James Mills Peirce became a professor of mathematics and astronomy at Harvard.<ref name= case /><ref name= out>{{cite web| url= http://outhistory.org/exhibits/show/aspectsofqueerexistence/aspectsofqueerexistencejamesmi| title= James Mills Peirce: 'Professor X'| website= outhistory.org| publisher= Digital Humanities Initiative, [[The New School]]| access-date= October 17, 2017}}</ref> He was first a Tutor in Mathematics, then a proctor at Harvard.<ref name= towards /> He was a preacher in [[Boston]] and [[Charleston, South Carolina]], but eventually returned to academia, first as Assistant Professor of Mathematics in 1861.<ref name= towards /> He was promoted to University Professor of Mathematics in 1869, then to [[Perkins Professorship of Astronomy and Mathematics|Perkins Professor of Astronomy and Mathematics]]—the same position his father once held—in 1885. He was head of the Graduate Department at Harvard from 1872 to 1895 (becoming its dean when it was converted to the Graduate School). He was the Dean of the [[Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences|Faculty of Arts and Sciences]] from 1895 to 1898.<ref name= towards />

Among his publications are ''Mathematical Tables Chiefly to Four Figures'' (1896)<ref name= out /> and ''A [[textbook|Text-Book]] of [[analytic geometry|Analytic Geometry]]; On the Basis of Professor Peirce's Treatise'' (1857).<ref name= case /> He was considered a world authority on [[quaternions]].

==Personal life==
Peirce was an early  proponent of homosexuality, writing extensively about gay love. "Sexual Inversion" ([[Studies in the Psychology of Sex Vol. 2|''Studies in the Psychology of Sex'' Vol. 2]], 1897)  by influential British sexologist [[Havelock Ellis]] contains in-depth case histories. It featured a letter by "Professor X." Circumstantial but suggestive evidence has identified the letter writer as Peirce. He wrote, "[W]e ought to think and speak of homosexual love, not as 'inverted' or 'abnormal' . . . but as being in itself a natural, pure and sound passion."<ref>{{Cite web |title=James Mills Peirce: "Professor X" · Aspects of Queer Existence in 19th-Century America, by Rich Wilson · OutHistory |url=https://outhistory.org/exhibits/show/aspectsofqueerexistence/aspectsofqueerexistencejamesmi |access-date=2023-06-26 |website=outhistory.org}}</ref>
